sections.title: Current conclusion
sections.markdown:
**Original census review, 31 October 2026:** The original 1841 Holly Walk census image has now been inspected through Findmypast: HO107/1135/14, folio 11, printed page 15, Leamington Priors. Robert is 65; Mary is entered with the Glasgow surname repeated by ditto and a Scotland birthplace mark. Mary’s final age digit remains ambiguous between 17 and 19: Findmypast transcribes 17, FreeCEN 19. Ann’s age also has an unresolved final digit (40/44; both providers transcribe 40). The schedule has no relationship column. These are readings of one census, not three independent family witnesses. The original does not prove Mary was Robert’s daughter or identify her with Mary Wilhelmina Campbell. Its 17/19 age reading still conflicts with the comparison bride’s 1816 birth and copied 1851 age 34. Keep that daughter-in-law comparison unselected and the existing father at 45%; Jane’s father remains 78%. No parent, identity, mother or vital-field change is made. The existing 1804 France birth fields remain unverified and conflict with the census, rather than being confirmed by it. A full original 1851 household and the 1839 marriage remain the discriminating identity tests.

Reviewed 31 October 2026: the Holly Walk household now has an exact census reference. Mary’s daughter relationship remains unproved; a daughter-in-law comparison with the younger Robert’s wife is now documented for testing. No child, parent or vital assessment changes.

sections.title: Earlier conclusion — newspaper identity review, 6 October 2026
sections.markdown: - [Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 1847-09-02, p.4](https://www.newspapers.com/image/401331272/): the late Robert Glasgow, Esq., of Montgreenan, county Ayr (father of both brides) — **strong** match. Unique designation 'of Montgreenan', described as 'the late' in Sept 1847. Of the Montgreenan owners: Dr Robert Glasgow-1076 died in 1827. Wikipedia says he had no offspring, but his own findings record natural children, including Anne, wife of Robertson-30564, so that is not a ground for exclusion; he remains a weaker possible alternative (corrected 7 October 2026; see `research/Glasgow-1076/findings.md`). Robert Robertson of Prenderguest, son-in-law, inherited in 1828 and took the name Glasgow; the LBS claim names 'Robert Glasgow Esq. (late Robertson) and Anne his wife'. His son Robert Robertson-Glasgow inherited in 1845 and lived to 1860 (thepeerage), so he cannot be 'the late' in 1847. Only Robertson-30564 survives. Sources: [Wikipedia: Montgreenan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgreenan); [UCL LBS claim 15 Feb 1836](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/claim/view/26620); [thepeerage p67979](https://ftp.thepeerage.com/p67979.htm)

sections.title: Source findings — UCL Legacies of British Slavery summary, copied 10 March 2025
sections.markdown:
The [UCL LBS entry for Robert Glasgow late Robertson](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/person/view/27300), as copied into the owner's earlier notes, gives his dates as 1775 to **27 January 1845** and reports, from an e-mail of Dr Anthony J. Cooke (9 February 2011), that he died at Pau, France, in 1845, his inventory being NRS **SC70/1/69/533**. It also records an Edinburgh MD (1797) and FRCS (1802), his marriage to Anne Glasgow on 2 August 1804, **four children: Robert the heir, Philadelphia Jane, Anne and Charlotte Marie Cecilia**, and an 1841 census household at Holly Walk, Leamington Priors, that includes Charlotte Robertson, aged 10.

Seen as: a copied catalogue summary, not inspected originals; the 1841 household is quoted from that summary. A death in January 1845 agrees with the son's succession in 1845 and with 'the late Robert Glasgow of Montgreenan' in September 1847. The named daughters Anne and Charlotte Marie Cecilia support his identification as father of the 1847 brides. Next record: NRS SC70/1/69/533.

Recorded in `archive/dump/TheGlasgows.md` (owner's checklist export of 10 March 2025); carried into this file on 7 October 2026.

sections.title: Record findings and identity limits — 17 October 2026
sections.markdown:
### Paisley double marriage, 1847

A notice published on 2 September 1847 reports two marriages at Paisley on the 25th ultimo, interpreted as 25 August. George Sherbrooke Airey, Royal Navy lieutenant and son of the late Lieutenant-General Sir George Airey, married Anne, second daughter of the late Robert Glasgow. At the same time Rev George Drake, son of Rev John Drake, rector of Stourton, married Charlotte Maria Cecilia, youngest daughter of the late Robert Glasgow of Montgreenan, Ayr. No mother is named. ([Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 2 September 1847, p. 4, marriages](https://www.newspapers.com/image/401331272/).)

The combination of the Montgreenan designation, Robert Robertson’s later Glasgow surname, death in 1845, and daughters Anne and Charlotte Marie Cecilia supports identification with this family. Charlotte’s distinctive full name and Drake married surname are especially strong. The newspaper directly states its father and spouse relationships; the profile assignments remain qualified and no mother is inferred.

Compatible family profiles are [Robert Robertson, later Glasgow](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Robertson-30564), [Anne Glasgow](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3000), [Charlotte Marie Cecilia Glasgow](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3003) and [Rev George Drake](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Drake-13873).

sections.title: Located census transcript and daughter-in-law comparison — 31 October 2026
sections.markdown:
The Holly Walk household now has a precise census locator: HO107/1135, enumeration district 10, folio 11, page 15, Leamington Priors (FreeCEN district Kenilworth). FreeCEN transcribes Mary Glasgow 19 and Wilhelmina Robertson 1, both born Scotland, with Robert Glasgow 65. It gives no relationship labels. This may be the source of the old copied WikiTree paragraph, so it is one census record, not independent family testimony.

A specific daughter-in-law alternative can now be tested. Paterson’s 1866 county history, printed pp. 513–514 (PDF 249–250), says the elder Robert’s eldest son and heir, born 22 May 1811, married Mary-Wilhelmina, daughter of John Campbell of Stonefield, on 11 July 1839; their children include Wilhelmina-Colquhoun. The checked existing bride is Campbell-38211 and groom Robertson-Glasgow-11. A married Mary beside the infant of this same family could be that daughter-in-law rather than another daughter of the household head. This is a new comparison, not an established identification.

The age problem remains real: FreeCEN gives Mary 19 in 1841, while Campbell-38211’s public profile gives 1816 and copies an 1851 age 34. The latter original is also unread. The infant’s full name and birth particulars are not established by FreeCEN. Paterson is a compiled family history, not an original marriage entry, and its adjacent Montgreenan descent narrative has known conflicts with the separately held court evidence. Do not transfer the book’s explicit John Campbell parentage to Glasgow-3021 before identifying the two Marys. Retain the selected Robert Robertson father at 45%, Jane’s father at 78%, all mother/vital fields and separate profiles; no father replacement, merge or confidence improvement is recorded.

Next discriminating test: inspect the original 1841 schedule at the exact locator, then the bride’s original 1839 marriage and 1851 household. Establish age, full name and family role before proposing John Campbell as Glasgow-3021’s father.

potential_parentage.method: Automated leads use birth surnames—not married surnames—as parental eligibility, role-specific biological age limits, bounded and approximate-date uncertainty, household chronology, specific time-aware localities, mapped distance, tenancy succession, migration destinations and sex-aware Scottish naming positions across generations. People already attached as the subject's parents stay in the identity summary and are excluded from this alternative-candidate list, regardless of relationship confidence. The main calibration uses clues available on disconnected profiles; existing parent and sibling links are retained as comparison context rather than treated as transferable evidence. Common ordered names and grandparent-to-child echoes receive a small non-zero weight, so a John or James match can support several independent criteria without producing a lead alone. Rare names, repeated bearers and bundles across otherwise distinct branches receive substantially more weight according to catalogue frequency. An exact migration place is weighted by its rarity and repetition across both branches; a shared destination country is worth only one point. Extra weight is added only when at least three independent clue types converge: naming, locality, specific migration, household chronology or collateral networks. Sparse profiles retain a clearly labelled chronology-only fallback instead of disappearing. Countries, states, counties and research clusters do not count as a shared locality, and fallback, broad representative or kin-inferred coordinates are excluded from distance scoring. Shared descendant profiles are removed before branch-name comparison. A candidate already recorded as a parent-in-law is excluded. A confident or independently supported parent is treated as settled; uncertain and unassessed attachments remain open to alternative comparison. A different linked parent, an uncle/aunt or grandparent path, and a matching existing child profile prevent an alternative from being classified as a strong direct-parent lead until the underlying tree conflict or duplicate is resolved. Familiar forms such as Bessie are normalised. Surname remains an eligibility filter worth zero points.
potential_parentage.warning: Naming customs, shared farms and occupations are circumstantial. Children, spouses and collateral relatives may be missing, and tree-derived family networks are not independent evidence. Scores rank research leads; they do not prove parentage.

=== Biography ===
=== Robert Glasgow (late Robertson) ===

'''Profile & Legacies Summary'''
*1775 - 27th Jan 1845*Robert Robertson, later known as Robert Glasgow, was the eldest son of Alexander Robertson of Gunsgreen House, Eyemouth. Initially titled "Esquire of Prenderguest," Robert was later designated "Esquire of Montgreenan" after inheriting the estates of his father-in-law, Dr. Robert Glasgow, in 1828<ref name="T71-892">T71/892, Counterclaim from Robert Glasgow Esq. and Anne his wife, withdrawn.</ref>. This inheritance included the Montgreenan estate in Ayrshire, Scotland, and the Mont Greenan and Sans Souci sugar plantations in St. Vincent<ref name="T71-1266">T71/1266, Marriage of Robert Robertson of Prenderguest to Anne Glasgow.</ref>. As per Dr. Glasgow's will, Robert changed his surname from Robertson to Glasgow<ref>Will of Robert Glasgow, 14/10/1828, Edinburgh Sheriff Court papers SC 6/44/4/1.</ref>.

==== Education and Professional Life ====
Robert Robertson graduated in Medicine from the University of Edinburgh in 1797 and became a Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1802<ref>List of the Graduates in Medicine in the University of Edinburgh from MDCCV to MDCCCLXVI (Edinburgh, Neil & Co., 1867).</ref>. Despite his professional background as a physician, his wealth and prominence derived primarily from the Glasgow family estates and plantations.

==== Marriage and Family ====
In 1804, Robert married Anne Glasgow, the illegitimate daughter and sole heir of Dr. Robert Glasgow<ref name="T71-1266"/>. Together, they had four children:
* '''Robert (1811-1860):''' Heir, a J.P. and advocate<ref name=RobertGrave>{{FindAGrave | 146731548 | sameas=no }}.</ref>.
* '''Philadelphia Jane.'''
* '''Anne.'''
* '''Charlotte Marie Cecilia (born 1827 in Rome):''' Charlotte’s baptism was recorded in Edinburgh on 20/07/1828<ref>GROS OPR Births 685/1 560 78.</ref>.

In 1841, Robert Glasgow was living at Holly Walk, Leamington Priors, with family members and several servants. His wife, Anne, was not listed in the census.<ref>1841 census online.</ref> Robert Glasgow died at Pau, France, in 1845, leaving behind an estate valued at £5,141, with arrears of £4,081 due from his father-in-law’s estate.<ref>Email from Dr. Anthony J Cooke (09/02/2011).</ref>.

==== Estates and Legacy ====
After inheriting Montgreenan and Sans Souci in 1828, Robert submitted claims for compensation under the Slave Compensation Act following the abolition of slavery in the British Empire. He was awarded:
* '''£6,987 4s 0d for Mont Greenan''' in St. Vincent<ref name="T71-892"/>
* '''£6,418 15s 6d for Sans Souci''' in St. Vincent<ref name="T71-1266"/>

==== Post-Abolition Challenges ====
Robert Glasgow, like many plantation owners, struggled to maintain profitability after the abolition of slavery. The Sans Souci estate had to diversify from sugar to crops like cocoa and bananas, although labor shortages persisted<ref>Anthony Cooke, 'An elite revisited: Glasgow West India merchants, 1783-1877', Journal of Scottish Historical Studies 32.2 2012 pp. 127-165.</ref>.
=== Further Information ===
* '''Absentee:''' Yes  
* '''British/Irish:''' Yes  
* '''Name in Compensation Records:''' Robert Robertson

==== Spouse ====
* Anne Glasgow

==== Children ====
* Anne (1805-)
* Robert (1811-1860)<ref name=RobertGrave/>
* Philadelphia Jane
* Charlotte Marie Cecilia (1827-)

==== Occupation ====
* Physician, plantation owner, landowner

==== Associated Claims ====
* '''St Vincent 466 (Mont Greenan):''' £6,987 4s 0d<ref name="T71-892"/>
* '''St Vincent 481A-C (Sans Souci):''' £6,418 15s 6d<ref name="T71-1266"/>

==== Relationships ====
* '''Husband → Wife:''' Anne Glasgow late Robertson (née Glasgow)
* '''Son-in-law → Father-in-law:''' Dr. Robert Glasgow
* '''Brother:''' George Home Robertson

==== Estates ====
* '''Montgreenan Estate:''' Ayrshire, Scotland. Inherited from Dr. Robert Glasgow in 1828.
* '''Sans Souci Estate:''' St. Vincent. Inherited in 1828, facing economic decline post-abolition.
* '''Gunsgreen House:''' Eyemouth, Berwickshire, Scotland. Inherited in 1804 from his father, Alexander Robertson.

==Sources ==
<references />

* T71/892, Counterclaim from Robert Glasgow Esq. and Anne his wife, withdrawn.
* Will of Robert Glasgow, 14/10/1828, Edinburgh Sheriff Court papers SC 6/44/4/1.
* T71/1266, Marriage of Robert Robertson of Prenderguest to Anne Glasgow.
* Cases Decided in the House of Lords: On Appeal from the Courts of Scotland 1836-37, Vol 2, pp. 333-34.
* Email from Dr. Anthony J Cooke (09/02/2011).
* University of Edinburgh Historical Alumni Database, http://collections.ed.ac.uk/alumni/record/91089 [accessed 06/01/2016].
* Burke's Landed Gentry (1837), Vol. I, p. 508.


== Acknowledgments ==
We are grateful to Derek Janes, Isla Tusk, and Anthony Cooke for their help with this entry.

== Research Notes ==
=== Paisley double marriage, 1847 ===

A notice published on 2 September 1847 reports two marriages at Paisley on the 25th ultimo, interpreted as 25 August. George Sherbrooke Airey, Royal Navy lieutenant and son of the late Lieutenant-General Sir George Airey, married Anne, second daughter of the late Robert Glasgow. At the same time Rev George Drake, son of Rev John Drake, rector of Stourton, married Charlotte Maria Cecilia, youngest daughter of the late Robert Glasgow of Montgreenan, Ayr. No mother is named.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/401331272/ Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 2 September 1847, p. 4, marriages].</ref>

The combination of the Montgreenan designation, Robert Robertson’s later Glasgow surname, death in 1845, and daughters Anne and Charlotte Marie Cecilia supports identification with this family. Charlotte’s distinctive full name and Drake married surname are especially strong. The newspaper directly states its father and spouse relationships; the profile assignments remain qualified and no mother is inferred.

Compatible family profiles are [[Robertson-30564|Robert Robertson, later Glasgow]], [[Glasgow-3000|Anne Glasgow]], [[Glasgow-3003|Charlotte Marie Cecilia Glasgow]] and [[Drake-13873|Rev George Drake]].
